subject: Copywriting
title: The Emotional Core
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Emotional Core.

hook.text: 'Because You're Worth It' doesn't mention shampoo. It speaks to self-worth.

buildup.text: L'Oréal's slogan, written by Ilon Specht in 1973, was a feminist statement. It told women they deserved luxury.

twist.text: The emotion must match the brand. 'Just Do It' is motivational for Nike but would be absurd for a funeral home.

climax.text: The greatest slogans tap into universal emotions: belonging, freedom, worth, adventure. The product is just the vehicle.

punchline.text: Touch an emotion, own a memory. Feelings outlast features.

details.summary: Every great slogan has an emotional core — a single feeling it evokes. Nike's 'Just Do It' taps into determination.  L'Oréal's 'Because You're Worth It' triggers self-worth. The best slogan writers identify the one emotion that matters most and build everything around it.
details.whyItMatters: People make decisions based on emotion, not logic. A slogan that hits the right emotional note creates an instant, visceral connection between the audience and the brand.
takeaways: The strongest slogans evoke a single dominant emotion
Emotional resonance drives recall more than clever wordplay
Identifying the core feeling requires deep audience understanding

faq.question: How do you find the emotional core of a slogan?
faq.answer: Start by asking what your audience fears, desires, or dreams about. Test candidate slogans by asking people what they feel — not think — when they hear each one. The slogan that consistently triggers the intended emotion is the winner.

faq.question: Can a slogan have more than one emotion?
faq.answer: Effective slogans focus on one primary emotion. Adding multiple feelings dilutes impact and creates confusion. Apple's 'Think Different' is purely about rebellious creativity — it doesn't try to also be warm, funny, or reassuring.
